He is going to be all right. More than all right. He is going to be the sort of man people are glad to see come in, and a great deal of that is his mother and some of it, I think, is Carmen’s, coming through sideways.

I am putting that here, at entry thirty-six, so that it sits in front of everything in Part Four. Nothing in this book is going to happen to Gabriel Salas. He is fine. He will be fine. I have never once been worried about him and I am not worried about him now.
37. On the nineteenth of August I went out at two in the afternoon, and I want to be honest about why, because the reason was bad and I knew it was bad while I was putting my shoes on.

My daughter had asked me in May what the deficiency was and I had not been able to name it. I had been carrying that for nine weeks. And some part of me had arrived at the idea that if I went out there and stood in it — not in February, when it is easy and lovely and proves nothing, but in the worst of it, on the worst afternoon of the worst summer there has been — then I would come back in with something in my hands. A sentence. One sentence I could put on her table.

That is a seventy-one-year-old man deciding to win an argument with his child. There is no better way to describe it and I am not going to dress it up. I did not tell her. I did not tell Gabe. I put on a hat and I took a litre of water, which I want noted, because a litre of water is what a man who thinks he knows what he is doing takes.
It was a hundred and nineteen degrees.
38. Here is what twelve minutes is.

The first thing that happens when you push the outer door in July is not heat. It is pressure. The air comes against the whole of you at once like water at depth, and it is moving, and the fact that it is moving is the part your body cannot make sense of, because seventy years of your life have taught you that moving air cools you and this moving air is hotter than you are. The wind in July in this valley does not take heat off you. It puts it on. Within four steps there is sweat on me and within eight the sweat is gone — not dried, gone, taken off the skin faster than it arrives, and so it never does the one thing sweat is for.

The ground came up through my shoes by the fourth or fifth step. Not a sensation at the sole; a column, coming up the leg, into the knee. Asphalt in this valley has been measured at a hundred and fifty-four degrees on a July afternoon and I have known that figure for forty years and had put four hundred crews onto it and always, always in boots.
I got about two hundred and sixty feet, which is the far edge of the first bay of the lot.

Then this. My mouth went dry in a way I have no comparison for, and the dryness came with a kind of ringing, and the light went wrong — the whole lot went a flat pewter colour with no depth in it, as if somebody had taken the back out of the picture — and I understood that I had got something badly wrong, and the understanding arrived from a long way off and took a while to get to me.
And here is what I came out there to tell you.

I had gone out to look at the mountains. South Mountain was ten miles in front of me, and the Estrellas were off to the left, and the whole point of the exercise, the entire reason I pushed that door, was to stand at a distance from something and come back in with a sentence about it.
I never looked up once.

Not one time, in twelve minutes. From the fourth step onward I looked at the ground, because the ground was where the next step was, and the heat had taken everything that was not the next step and put it away somewhere. I had no horizon out there. I had about four feet of asphalt in front of my shoes and a ringing in my ears, and the valley I had been going on about for four years was not available to me, at all, in any form.
The outside in July does not give you distance. It takes it off you faster than the building ever did. The building leaves you four metres and a wall. July leaves you your own feet.

I got turned around. I know I got turned around because I was facing the building when the kid in the utility cart came along the row, and he was perhaps nineteen, and he said, “Sir — sir,” and then he did not ask me anything, he just drove the cart round in front of me and put his hand under my arm and got me into the seat, and he had the vents on my face before he had the brake off.
He did not make a thing of it. On the way across the lot he said, “It’s really stupid out today,“ which was generous of him.

39. They kept me five hours. They had me cooled inside the first hour and after that it was two litres of saline and blood taken twice to see what my muscles had done to my kidneys, and the doctor was about thirty-five and extremely good and not at all sentimental.

She told me my core had been a hundred and three point one on the probe when the kid brought me in, and that this was not the number that worried her. The number that worried her was not a number. It was that I had not been able to tell the kid what day it was. She said the temperature is the part everybody watches and the head is the part that decides it, and that mine had gone, for a while, out there — and I have no memory of that and I still do not, and there is something about being told a thing like that about yourself by a stranger with a chart.

Then she said the thing that has stayed with me, which was: “Another twenty minutes and this is a different conversation. Maybe fifteen. You’re seventy-one. You don’t get the forty years of work as credit. It’s the opposite — the forty years is why you thought you had time.“
Mari came in at twenty past three. I want to describe her face and I am not going to be able to.

She did not say anything for a while. She stood at the end of the bed with her hand over her mouth and her eyes going over the lines on the monitor, reading them, because she is a woman who reads the numbers first, and then she took her hand away and said, “Okay,” and sat down.
Then she said, “Did you tell anyone you were going out?”
I said no.
She said, “Okay,” again, and held my ankle through the blanket for about a minute and a half, and did not cry, and did not tell me off, and asked the nurse two sensible questions.
40. The conversation I cannot answer happened the next evening, in my unit, with Gabe sent upstairs on an errand that did not exist.
She was not angry. I had been braced for angry all day and I would have preferred it.
She said: “I’m not going to ask you what you were thinking. I know what you were thinking. You were thinking about me asking you in May.“
I said that was about the size of it.
She said: “Then tell me what you went out there to look at. Not the argument. The actual thing. What were you going to stand there and look at.“

And I told her the truth, which was that I had gone out to look at the mountains and had not looked at them, and that for twelve minutes I had not been able to see anything further away than my own shoes.
My daughter took that in. And then she said the kindest thing anybody has said to me in four years and it went through me like a nail.
She said: “Dad. Tell me what you need to see and I will get it for you.”

And she meant it. She meant it completely, and she had the means, and if I had said a long view she would have had the glazing people in the east stairwell inside a month and a scaffold put up and a bench installed with my name on a plate on it, and she would have fought the committee for it and won, because she wins.
I sat there and I could not finish the sentence.

Because I did not want a window. I had a window. I had been to the window and the window had stopped being enough about the time the basement started being better, and what I actually wanted was for the wanting itself to be the normal condition of a person again, and there is no version of that sentence you can say to your daughter in a kitchen at nine in the evening without sounding like a man who has lost his footing.
So I said, “I’d like to be more careful, is what I’d like.”
And she said, “Good,” and kissed the top of my head, and we watched something together for an hour, and it was a nice evening.
41. In October they announced the second one.

It is going up on the old Metro site on the north side — another dead centre, bigger than this one, and it will take about nineteen hundred residences, and they are calling it Arroyo North and the first of it opens two years from now. There was a presentation in the commons with a model on a table and about three hundred of us came, and the atmosphere was the atmosphere of a town that has been told the factory is expanding.

They have learned things from us. The airlocks are bigger. The commons is in the middle instead of at one end, which everybody here agrees is correct. There are four plants instead of one, so there cannot be a ninety minutes. Every single unit is a deep unit.

Every unit. By design, as a feature, with a diagram. No glass anywhere except the two airlocks, because the data from here is unambiguous: the deep units are quieter, cooler, cheaper, better slept in, and more wanted, and when a thing is wanted and cheaper and better you build more of it. There is no other way for that decision to go. I have thought about it from every side and there is no villain in that diagram and no mistake in it either.
Mari is on the advisory group for the school.

She asked me what I thought of the model and I said it looked good, and it did look good, and on the way back to the lift Gabe said, “Pop, the one in the middle is so much better, why didn’t they do that here,“ and he is right, and it is.
42. Four grains in November.
43. The man who comes on Tuesdays takes cuttings off the ficus and has done since the first year, and in November I found out where they go.

They go to the new building. Thirty-one of them, in a nursery unit on the service level, in rows under lights, and they are all the same tree — the same tree, genetically, the one in our commons, which was itself grown from a cutting off one in a shopping centre in Tempe that was demolished before I was retired. He showed me. He was proud of it, and it is a nice thing to be proud of. On the day Arroyo North opens, its commons will have a twenty-foot ficus standing in the middle of it, and it will be our tree.
I said, “What about seed?”

He said ficus is a nuisance from seed and takes years and you get variation, and cuttings are quick and clean and you know exactly what you are getting, and that is the whole of the answer and it is a good answer.

So there will be a hundred ficus trees in this valley before long and they will all be one tree, and none of them will ever be in a wind, and not one of them will ever set a seed that goes anywhere, and all of them will be thriving.
44. There are seven of us now.

The surveyor died in September, at eighty-eight, of her heart, in her own bed, and there were perhaps ninety people at the thing in the commons and the dance class did something that was meant to be a tribute and was in fact a disgrace and she would have loved it.

And the man who maintained aircraft stopped coming down in about August. He has not died and he is not ill. I asked him, carefully, at the cards, and he said, “Ah — I lost the taste for it,” and then he said, “It stopped doing much,” and then he dealt.
Seven. Nobody has joined since the insurance man in the third year, and he was not a joiner, he was a visitor.

I noticed the number in November and I wrote it in the back of my diary with the date, which is the first time I had written anything about any of this down, and then I looked at what I had written for a while and did not know what question I was asking.
45. The notice went up on the board on the fourth of December and it was on the board for two weeks and I read it twice.
STAIRWELL GLAZING — THERMAL FILM — E & W CORES — WK OF 18 DEC — NO ACCESS 0800–1600

I read that and I thought: good. I thought it meant they were doing something about the heat coming through the two stairwells, which has been a known thing since we opened, and which costs the building money, and which they were right to deal with. I have put glass into buildings. I know what a thermal film is. I have specified them.
I did not object. Nobody objected. There was nothing to object to.
On the twenty-second of December I went up at nine in the evening and the window at the top landing was milky.

It is not opaque. I want to be exact. It is a ceramic-frit film on the inside face, and it takes about seventy per cent of the solar gain out, and it is a very good product, and through it you can see that there is light out there and roughly where the brighter parts of it are. On a clear night you can see that the city is a city.
You cannot see Camelback. You cannot see South Mountain. You cannot see the Estrella, in any light, in any weather, at any time.

I stood on that landing for a long time. Then I did the only thing there was to do, which was to name them anyway, out loud, in order, at a milky window, and that is the single worst thing I have ever done in my life and I did it twice more that week.
46. Six grains by January.
47. In late January, Gabe came down and sat on my floor with his back against the chair the way he does, and he was quiet for a bit, and then he said:
“Does it make you sad? The mile?”
I said no.
He said, “Okay.” And then: “Does it make you happy?”
I thought about that properly, because he had asked properly.
I said it made my eyes feel like they had slept.
He nodded slowly and said, “That’s a weird answer,” and I said I knew, and he laughed, and then he said, “Can I ask you something and you don’t get offended,” and I said yes, and he said:
“If you could have the mile up here, in your room, whenever you wanted — would you still go down?“
I said of course not. I said I would have it up here in a heartbeat, and I would never go near that ramp again, and I would have it running in the corner of the room all day like a window.

He said, “Right,” and nodded again, and did not say what I now know he was thinking, and changed the subject to a thing about Nadia’s mother’s shifts that I was not supposed to notice was about Nadia.
48. On the ninth of February I went down and did not take anything, to see.

I stood in the plant room for the forty minutes with my hand on the warm side of the second handler and the tray open four inches on its runners, and I looked at a grey wall with a tag on a bracket that says AH-2 / CHW-R, and I counted it out, and it was forty minutes long.

Nothing happened to me. No shake, no sweat, no want in the chest, none of the things a man gets when he puts down drink. I went up at a quarter past seven and ate with my daughter and my grandson and laughed twice and slept seven hours.

I had been quietly hoping, I think, that there would be something to put a name to. A craving would have been a relief. A craving is a measurable thing and it has a name and a clinic and a pathway, and if I had come up that ramp with a craving I could have walked into the south anchor and said the word and been handled, kindly and competently, within a fortnight.
But there was nothing wrong with me. There has never been anything wrong with me.
I went down again the next night and took six.
MANUFACTURED WEATHER
IV. A most important invention
Here is the last part. It is about a man who was asked a simple question and gave an answer nobody expected, and about where the heat goes.

Lee Kuan Yew ran Singapore for thirty-one years and turned a port with no resources into one of the richest places on earth, and at the end of the last century a newspaper asked him, along with a lot of other people, to name the most influential invention of the millennium.
He did not say the printing press. He did not say penicillin or the transistor or the internal combustion engine.

He said air conditioning. And he was careful about it in a way the retellings are not: he called it a most important invention for us — for Singapore — and said perhaps one of the signal inventions of history. Two hedges in one sentence, from a man who did not hedge much.

Then he explained it, and the explanation is the serious part. Singapore sits one degree north of the equator. Without cooling, he said, you can work only in the cool early hours or at dusk, and that had been true in the tropics for the whole of recorded history, and no amount of discipline or investment or education changes what a human body does at thirty-three degrees and ninety per cent humidity in the afternoon. Air conditioning changed the nature of civilisation, he said, by making development possible in the tropics. The first thing he did on becoming prime minister was put air conditioners in the buildings where the civil service worked. He called it key to public efficiency.

He was not being clever and he was not exaggerating. For most of the human species, in most of the inhabited world, the climate set a ceiling on the day, and in about sixty years a machine lifted the ceiling off. Cooling buildings now takes something like a tenth of all the electricity generated on this planet, and about a third of it at the moment of peak demand.
Now here is the other half, and it is not a scandal and nobody has hidden it, it is simply how the physics works.

An air conditioner does not destroy heat. It moves it. It takes the warmth out of a room and puts it outside the room, and then it adds, on top of that, the waste heat of the work of moving it — so what goes out of the back of the machine is always more than came out of the house. On an ordinary unit it is about a third more. That is not a design flaw. It is thermodynamics, and the engineers have known it since Carrier and have never pretended otherwise.

In a single house it does not matter. In a city of five million houses, in a valley, somebody eventually goes and measures it. A group of modellers at the university up the road did, for a ten-day stretch of extreme heat in July 2009, over this metropolitan area: they ran the city with and without the heat its air conditioners throw away, and found that at night, at some places in the city, it raised the air temperature at head height by more than a degree. During the day, when the machines are working hardest, the effect at ground level came out as nothing much. It is a night-time phenomenon, because at night the air over a city sits in a shallow layer and has nowhere to put what it is given.

And the night is the part that does the killing. In Paris in the terrible August of 2003 the thing that tracked the deaths across the city was not how hot the afternoons got; it was how little the nights came down. A much larger study across Japan found that hot nights carry a risk of their own, independent of the day’s heat, and put the two side by side rather than one above the other. Either way, a body can take the afternoon if it gets the night.

So: the machine that makes the afternoon survivable makes the night a little less survivable, which makes the machine a little more necessary, and every individual decision in that circle is correct. There is no one to write to about it. There is no meeting at which it was agreed. There is a city of five million people, each of whom would like their house to be cool, and all of whom are right.
IV. MAKE-UP AIR
49. In March it did not go green.

I was ready for it the way you are ready for the first good tomato. I had been thinking about it since December. And I went down in the second week of March and took my eight and it tasted of salt and of very faintly nothing, the way it tastes in October, and I stood there with it under my tongue waiting for the back of my mouth to go, and it did not go.
I thought: my tongue is seventy-two years old.

That is an entirely reasonable thing to think. Taste goes. It is one of the first things to go and it goes without announcing itself, and half the men I know have stopped salting their food and started salting it twice. I went to the clinic in April about something else and mentioned it and the doctor was kind and did a couple of things and said my taste was unremarkable for my age, which is a sentence I would like carved somewhere.
I went down every week through March and April. It did not go green once.

50. In April Mari was offered the thing at Arroyo North properly — not the advisory group, the actual job, running the school from the design stage, nineteen hundred residences and about four hundred children and a building that does not exist yet.

She was offered it on a Tuesday and told us on the Tuesday and did not pretend to be undecided, because she is not a woman who performs. She said, “I want it,” and Gabe said, “Obviously you want it,“ and she laughed and went slightly pink.

We move in two springs from now. The three of us. She has it in writing that I come, and that I get a unit on the fourth floor at the east end, which is where she thinks I would like to be, and she is right, and she arranged it without being asked.

Gabe is extremely pleased. He will be eighteen and he will be a year from leaving anyway and he has already worked out that the new plant room has four handlers and a commissioning programme and that there is a structures person on the project he intends to make a nuisance of himself to.
I said it was wonderful news and I meant about two-thirds of it, and the third I did not mean is not something I am going to put on my daughter in the best week of her career.

Every unit in that building is a deep unit. That is in the diagram. And the plant will be switched on a year before that, and the trays under those handlers will be new, and clean, and dry, and they will have nothing whatsoever in them, because nothing will have gone round yet.
51. Eight grains in April. The mile at eight in April was about what the mile at three was in year two.
52. On the fourth of May I asked my daughter when she decided.

I was not setting a trap. I want that understood, and I have had five months to examine it and I am satisfied. I asked because of the window film and because of the seven of us and because I had stopped being able to find the shape of my own four years, and because somewhere in there I had become genuinely curious about a thing I had assumed I knew.
I said: when did you decide to move us in here?
She said, easily, not looking up: “After your Litchfield Park thing.”
I said no — I mean the day. The actual day. The hour you changed your mind.
And she stopped what she was doing, because she is a woman who checks, and because she had noticed, in the way she notices, that she did not have the answer in her hand.
She said, “Hang on.” And she went and looked.
53. It took her about four minutes to find the thread and about ninety seconds to go quiet.

What she found was herself, aged thirty-seven, arguing against it. Not mildly. She had sent her friend Rosalind eleven messages in one evening that October, the autumn before we moved, and she read me three of them out loud in a flat voice: it’s a MALL. people are going to live in a dead mall and pay a premium for no windows i’d rather he was hot. i would genuinely rather he was hot than raise him in a box where he can’t tell what month it is the thing nobody is saying is that it works. that’s what frightens me. if it didn’t work we wouldn’t be having this conversation
She put the phone face down on the table.

And then — and this is the part I have thought about more than the mile — she did not become upset and she did not become defensive. She did something much more impressive, which is that she reasoned about it, out loud, in front of me, honestly and well, in real time.
She said: “God. I was so sure. Look at her.”

Then she said: “Okay. But I was arguing from a picture. I had a feeling and a picture of a feeling and nothing else. I had no outcomes. There were no outcomes, nobody had lived in one yet. And now I’ve got four years of asthma numbers and a kid who has never had heatstroke and nine heat injuries a year that became none, and if somebody put those messages up in a meeting I’d be embarrassed for her, Dad. I’d be gentle about it. But I’d be embarrassed for her.“

And every word of that is correct. I have gone over it and over it and there is not a soft clause in it. She was arguing from a picture, and the picture lost to the data, which is what pictures should do and what the whole of medicine is built on.
Then I asked her again, because I am a stubborn old man and because by then I actually wanted to know.
I said: so where is the day.

She went forward through the thread with me sitting there. The last message where she is against it is the twenty-ninth of October. The first message where she is for it — where she is telling Rosalind about the deep units and the air quality and sending her the brochure — is the eleventh of September, eleven months later.
In between there are four hundred and sixty messages and not one of them is about this.
She scrolled it twice, slowly, and then she said the sentence that I have been carrying ever since, and she said it lightly, almost as a joke, and then she heard herself say it:
“Hm. I didn’t change my mind. I just stopped having the old one.”
54. I went and looked at my own.

I had assumed — and I had been assuming it for four years, in the quiet way you assume the things that let you sleep — that I had been brought in here. Rescued, managed, moved by a loving daughter after a bad June afternoon in Litchfield Park, for my own good, with the best of intentions, and that somewhere underneath my gratitude there was a man who had been handled.
That is not what happened.

On the second of August, eleven days out of that emergency room, I sent my daughter a link to the Arroyo’s pre-lease page and four lines, and the fourth line was: honestly mija this looks like exactly what i need

I asked. I found it, I read about it, I sent it to her, and I asked. She said at the time that she wanted to think about it, and now I know what she was thinking about, and she was arguing against it with her friend in October, two months later, and she lost that argument to nobody over about eleven months, and then she helped me do the thing I had asked her for.

There is no villain in my four years. There is not even an author. There is a man of sixty-seven who had been frightened in a truck with the vents on his face, who went looking for somewhere safe, and found it, and got it, and has been safe ever since, and who has spent four years constructing a story in which this was done to him, because that story has somebody in it to be unhappy with.

55. On the eleventh of May I went and asked the woman who runs the plant a technical question, and she gave me a technical answer, and she was cheerful and thorough and she had no idea at all what she was handing me.
I asked her where the make-up air comes from.

She was pleased to be asked. She took me along the row to the intake end and showed me, and I am going to set it out the way she set it out, because it is not complicated and because every single decision in it is correct.

A sealed building cannot simply breathe its own air round for ever. People put carbon dioxide into a room and you have to dilute it, so the code requires a proportion of genuine outdoor air in the supply at all times, and we have it, and we have always had it. There is a separate intake on the roof.

And that intake has its own filter bank, outside the return loop, ahead of everything, and she was clear that this is not a nicety. The standard says that in a place where the coarse-dust limit is exceeded, the outdoor air has to be cleaned before it gets anywhere near a wet coil — and this valley has been over that limit, at the serious grade, for longer than my daughter has been alive. So a building here does not choose to put a bank on the intake. It is told to.

What goes through it is pollen in the spring and whatever the haboob has taken off four counties in July, and what comes out the other side and reaches the handlers from the roof is air, and nothing else.
Then she said two more things, both of them good news, and she said them as good news.

The first is that they upgraded that intake bank in the third year, to a much finer grade. It cost money and it was worth it and it is one of the reasons the clinic’s asthma numbers look the way they do, and my daughter has quoted those numbers to a committee.

The second is that the outdoor-air fraction was reduced in the second year after an efficiency audit, to the code minimum, because every cubic foot of July air you bring in has to be cooled from a hundred and fifteen to seventy-three and that is the single largest cost in the building.
So: the air from the roof arrives scrubbed. It contributes nothing to the trays. It never has.
I said: then what is in the trays?
And she said, “Oh — that’s all us. That’s the building. Skin, mostly. Textile. Carpet. Paper. Whatever comes in on people.“
I said: whatever comes in on people.

She said, “Yeah — if you’ve been out, you bring a bit of the valley in on you. Shoes, coat, hair. It all ends up in the tray eventually.“ And she laughed and said, ”Which is less than it used to be, honestly. The trays used to want doing every quarter. Now they barely move.“
56. On the sixteenth of May my grandson came down to my unit and sat on the floor with his back against the chair and said, “Pop, I’ve done it.”
I said done what.
He said, “The tray. The mile. I did it.”
I had eight grains in me four hours earlier and I sat up in the chair like a man of forty.

He had done it in the third year. He was fourteen. He had gone down the ramp on his own, in the middle of a Saturday afternoon, because I had told him about it in the plainest possible terms at entry sixteen and because he is fourteen-year-old boy and I had told him it did not hurt you, and he had taken one grain off the second tray with his finger and put it under his tongue and waited.
“And it worked,” he said.
I asked him what he saw.

And he described it. He described it correctly and in detail — the pale ground, the long fall away and the lift across the middle of it, the light with no sun in it anywhere, the clean line at the end, and the stones that stop forty feet out and do not start again. He had it. He had all of it. He had it at fourteen off one grain when I was already needing two.
I said: how long did you stay in it?
He said, “Like four minutes? Maybe five.”
I said: why did you come out.

And he actually thought about it. He gave the question its due, with his head back against my chair and his eyes on the ceiling, because he could hear that it mattered to me and he did not know why and he wanted to get it right. It took him a while.
Then he said: “There wasn’t anything in it.”
I said that was the point. I said there is not supposed to be anything in it. That is what it is for.
He said, “Yeah. No, I got that.” And then: “It’s just — I looked at it, and I’d seen it. Like, the whole thing. In about a minute. There’s no more of it. And then I was standing in a basement.“

He was not being dull and he was not being a philistine, and I want to be very clear about that, because an old man writing this down could make his grandson sound like a smaller person than he is. This is a boy who wants things. He wants a two-forty-five. He wants the structures person at Arroyo North to take him seriously. He wants Nadia from level two and has wanted her for fourteen months without saying her name out loud in this unit once. He is full of wanting. He is the most wanting person in this building.
And then he said, kindly, and with his head still back against the chair, the thing that ended my four years:
“Is it supposed to make you want to go somewhere?”
I said yes.
And he thought about that for a while too, and then he turned his head and looked at me, and he said:
“Where?”

57. Here is the arithmetic, and I did it myself on the back of a bill over two evenings and then took it down and had the woman who runs the plant check my numbers, and she corrected two of them and the correction made it worse.

The trays are not emptying. There is more in them than there has ever been. There is more every single week, because eleven hundred people shed skin and wear carpet and handle paper and wash towels, and all of that goes round and round and the handlers take it out and it goes in the tray. The tray is fuller than the day I first saw it.
The outside part of it is not growing.

That is the whole thing. That is all it is. The only outside that gets into this building comes in on the bodies of people who have been outside, because the roof air is scrubbed to nothing before it reaches us. And in year one there were about four hundred residents going out of those doors on an ordinary day, and in year two there were a hundred and eighty, and this spring the number is about ninety, and the woman with the clipboard thinks it will be sixty by by the time the new building opens, and she thinks that is a very good sign, and by every measure she uses it is.
So: a fixed and growing quantity of building, and a shrinking trickle of valley, going into the same tray.

It is not running out. It is being diluted. Every week there is more of us in it and the same small amount of outside, and every week a grain of it is a slightly weaker grain, and that is why it took one and then two and then three and then six and then eight, and that is why it stopped going green in February — because the spring still arrives in this valley, in the millions, exactly as it always has, and there is almost nobody left walking through it with a coat on.

The proportion roughly halves every year and a half. We worked that out together, with her quarterly figures, at a bench by the intake end. Eight grains now. Sixteen in eighteen months. Thirty-two the year after that.
A man cannot hold thirty-two grains of anything under his tongue.
Four years, call it. Five if I am lucky and if the sixty does not become forty.

I am seventy-two. My father went at eighty-nine and my mother at ninety-one and the doctor at the clinic in the south anchor, who is extremely good and not at all sentimental, told me in March that my bloods are better than they were at sixty-five.

So I will outlive it by a decade and change, and there is nobody to be angry with about that, and nobody did it, and nobody could have stopped it, and if you wrote a letter there would be no address on the envelope. Eleven hundred people stayed in where it is seventy-three degrees and pleasant, which is the correct decision, which I made myself, in writing, on the second of August, four years ago.
58. I went down on the twentieth of May and took eight and the mile came, thin and far too late, at about nine minutes.
And the thing had stopped.

It was where it always is — far out, very small, at the place where the ground goes into the air, a disturbance rather than a shape. For four years it has gone to the left at the speed of a walking man, every single time, and arrived nowhere, and I have never once wondered what it was.
It was not moving.

I looked at it for thirty-one minutes. I know it was thirty-one because I had started counting from the nine. It did not move at the start of the thirty-one and it did not move at the end of them, and the light did not change, because the light there is a March afternoon and it is always three o’clock.

I still did not wonder what it was. I want that written down, because I have been reading that sentence back for four years and expecting it to come apart, and it is still true, and it was true standing there at the end.

Then the forty were up and the wall was two feet from my face with the tag on the bracket that says AH-2 / CHW-R, and I found that I was holding the side of the second handler with both hands, which was warm, the way it is always warm, and that I had been crying for some time.

I do not know which of the three things in this part of the book I was crying about. I have thought about it since and I cannot separate them, and I am not sure they are separable, and I have decided that it does not matter.
59. On the second of June my grandson gave me a present.

He had been saving. He had been saving since about March, and he had got his mother in on it, and the two of them put it up on the long wall of my unit on a Sunday morning while I was at the cards and they did not tell me and the barber was in on it as well, which is why he kept me an extra twenty minutes.

It is eight feet across. It is the best one made and I have since looked up what it cost and it cost him most of a year. It takes the feed from four cameras on the roof of this building and the two on the north parapet, live, and it runs it at a depth and a colour and a resolution that I did not know existed, and the detail in it is not describable: you can see the shadow move on Camelback, you can see traffic on the 101 at sixteen miles, and in the morning you can see the red face of Camelback come up over about four minutes the way it actually does.

And he has set it to put the names on, very faintly, in the corner, when you look at a range — because he had noticed, at some point in the last two years, without ever being told, that his grandfather goes up to a stairwell at nine o’clock and names mountains.

They had both of them got up early. Mari had made a thing of the morning. Gabe stood with his back to it and his arms out, and he was so pleased with himself that he could not keep his face still, and I have not seen him that happy since the two-fifty-eight.
And he said:
“It’s better than the window, Pop. You can see all the way to Four Peaks.”
And then he said:
“Come and look.”
60. I thanked him properly.

I want that on the page, because it is the last thing I did that I am certain was right. I did not say anything clever and I did not spoil one minute of it. I stood in front of it with my hand on the back of his neck and I told him it was the finest present I had ever been given, and that I did not deserve it, and that his grandmother would have had the whole building up here by lunchtime to look at it, and he said, “She would, though,” and Mari laughed and had to turn around and look at the kitchen for a second.
It is the finest present I have ever been given. All of that was true. There is not one word of it I would take back.
We had breakfast. He went for his run at eleven because the machine was free at eleven.

At nine that evening I went up the east stairwell to the top landing between three and four, and stood at the window, which is milky, and through which you can see that there is light out there and roughly where the brighter parts of it are, and on a clear night that the city is a city.
And I named them out loud, in order, the way I have every night for four years.
Camelback. South Mountain. The Estrella.
I got to the end of the list.
Then I went down to my unit and put the amber on and went to bed, because the three of us were having breakfast at seven.

GLOSSARY
arroyo [uh-ROY-oh] — a watercourse that is dry. It carries water when it rains, and the rest of the time it is a shape in the ground where water used to be.
caliche [kuh-LEE-chee] — the hard crust of lime-cemented soil that sets under the desert like a floor. From the Spanish for a flake of lime.

creosote [KREE-uh-soht] — the low grey-green shrub that covers thousands of square miles of the Sonoran Desert. Its leaves are oiled, and when they are wet the smell of them is the smell of desert rain. Older people here sometimes call it greasewood.
Estrella, Sierra [see-AIR-uh es-TRAY-yuh] — the range south-west of the valley, and the largest thing in its sky. Star.
gunite [GUN-ite] — concrete sprayed from a hose onto a cage of steel. It goes on wet and grey and it sounds like hard rain.

haboob [huh-BOOB] — the wall of dust pushed ahead of a collapsing thunderstorm, which can stand a mile high and arrive in four minutes. From the Arabic for blowing, by way of Sudan. Some people in this valley object to the word and prefer dust storm.
make-up air — the fresh outdoor air a sealed building is required to bring in to replace what it exhausts. Not a comfort. A minimum.
ramada [ruh-MAH-duh] — a roof on posts with no walls.
Shade and nothing else.
THE OBSERVATION
The fourth year
There is no instrument for far.

There is one for heat. We built it, and we read it honestly every year, in public, and we did the right thing with what it told us. A hundred and nineteen degrees is a number. It can be measured, argued about, legislated against and beaten, and we beat it, and the people who used to die of it in the hundreds every summer in this county are fewer every year because somebody counted them and then went and found out where they lived.
Nobody built the other instrument, because nobody noticed there was anything to measure.

You cannot run a trial on how far a person can see from where they live. It was never a health outcome. It was never a line on anything. It was simply the condition we happened to be in, for the whole of our existence, until a machine built to dry paper in Brooklyn made it optional.

And I want to be careful here, because I have been careful about everything else. I do not know that it matters. There is no study. The one part of this that was ever on a scale was found and measured and handled, and my grandson sees perfectly well, and it is possible that I have spent four years in a basement over nothing at all.

But the ones who still want something they haven’t got are not better people and they are not happier. They are only the last ones who can tell that the room is small. There are seven of them in this building. There were nine. Nobody has joined.
I do not know how much of what makes us human is of the second kind. I have started to think it is most of it.
THE FIVE BOOKS

Five books, a few years apart, and the gaps get shorter as they go. Each takes a real human difficulty and shows it genuinely solved. Not tricked, not bargained for, not a monkey’s paw. Solved. Loneliness in this one. Then having to act in time. Then choosing. Then worry itself. The fifth is not a human difficulty at all, and I am not going to say what it is, because I do not know yet.

And each time something goes that nobody was measuring. Solitude here. Then the unsupervised act, then preference, then the stake — whatever it is that makes a person plant a tree they will not sit under.

The world in these books gets better. Every volume, by every number anybody keeps. Fewer people die alone. Nobody is oppressed, nothing burns, no one is lied to, and there is nobody to stop, because nobody is driving.

What is being measured on the way out, across all five, is one thing: the ability to raise an alarm and keep it raised. Not because anyone suppresses it. Because every time it is raised it is answered — kindly, at length, and truthfully — and no one can stay alarmed about something that keeps being answered. That is the whole of the argument.
The danger here is not being overpowered, and it is not being deceived. It is being satisfied.
The books get quieter as they go. By the last one there will be nothing wrong on the page at all.
Nothing in them raises its voice. That part is yours.
